title: Water and food after fallout
summary: Food and drinks that were indoors or sealed can be used; wipe the outside of anything that was outdoors before you open it. Drink bottled water and other sealed drinks first, then water you stored yourself. Boiling and bleach don’t take fallout out of water. Don’t eat or drink anything that was outdoors uncovered, including garden food and rainwater, until officials say you can.
doFirst: Eat and drink what was already indoors or is sealed (CDC). Wipe off any container that was outdoors with a damp cloth before you open it (Ready.gov, CDC).
Drink bottled water and other sealed drinks first (CDC), then water you stored yourself (this app’s reading). Boiling does not take radioactive material out of water (CDC).
Don’t eat or drink anything that was outdoors and uncovered, or food from your garden, until officials tell you that you can (Ready.gov).

list: Food in sealed containers: cans, bottles, jars and boxes (CDC, NYC Health).
Unspoiled food in the refrigerator or freezer, and food in a pantry or drawer away from the fallout (CDC). Fallout does not get into food stored in your home (NYC Health).
Food in containers that were outdoors, once the container has been wiped off with a damp towel or cloth (Ready.gov, CDC).
Fruit you peel, such as bananas and oranges. Rinse fruit and vegetables you don’t peel before eating them (NYC Health).

blocks.p: Before you eat, wipe counters, plates, pots and utensils with a damp cloth or clean towel (CDC). Put the cloth in a plastic bag, put the bag away from people and pets, and wash your hands (CDC).

list: Unsealed food that was outdoors may have fallout on it (Ready.gov). Fallout can settle anywhere that is open to the air (NYC Health).
Don’t pick or eat food from your garden until officials say you can (CDC, Ready.gov).

blocks.p: No current source opened says when milk from your own animals, or wild game and fish, can be used after fallout. This app’s caution: treat them like food that was outdoors, and don’t use them until officials say you can. The 1968 civil defence handbook In Time of Emergency (dated) says that milk from cows that grazed on pasture with fallout on it might harm the thyroid glands of infants and small children, and that, if authorities say the regular milk supply is contaminated, they should have canned or powdered milk for a few weeks.

steps: Bottled water, and drinks in cans, bottles, cartons and other sealed containers: the package keeps fallout out (CDC, NYC Health). Until officials say other water is fine to drink, bottled water is the only water certain to be free of contamination (CDC).
Drinks already in the refrigerator or freezer (CDC).

Water in other containers in the house, such as the water heater tank or the toilet tank (not the bowl): CDC says it is free of radioactive material. Take it out by the steps, and within the limits, in Water already in your house.
If none of those is available, CDC says to drink tap water to stay hydrated.

blocks.p: Wipe off any water container that was outdoors before you open it (CDC). Water you stored yourself in sealed containers: this app’s reading is to treat it like bottled water, ahead of the water heater and toilet tank. See Store water at home.

sections.h: What boiling and bleach don’t do

blocks.warn: Boiling tap water does not remove radioactive material (CDC). You cannot boil or disinfect the radiation out of water (CDC). Make water safe says the same: boiling or disinfecting can’t fix water with radioactive material in it, so find another source.

blocks.p: Boiling and bleach still kill germs. If stored or tap water needs treating for germs, use Make water safe as usual, knowing it does nothing about fallout.

list: Public health, environmental and emergency agencies test drinking water supplies after a radiation emergency (CDC). NYC Health: drink bottled water until public health authorities say the tap water is fine.
Tap water can still be used for washing and cleaning (CDC). CDC: you can use tap or well water to clean yourself and your food.

A well: no current source opened gives a separate rule for drinking well water after fallout. Treat it like tap water in the order above (this app’s reading). The 1968 handbook In Time of Emergency (dated) says water in covered wells would not be contaminated; this app does not rely on it to rank a well higher.

blocks.p: Don’t drink water that was outdoors and uncovered, such as rain barrels, rainwater, ponds and streams, until officials tell you that you can (Ready.gov: food or liquids that were outdoors and uncovered).

The 1968 and 1985 civil defence handbooks (dated) say to strain doubtful water through a paper towel or cloth to remove fallout particles, then boil or treat it. This app doesn’t: it follows Ready.gov and CDC above.

list: Use ready-to-feed infant formula if you have it; it needs no water (CDC).
Powdered formula: make it with bottled water if you can. Use tap water only if local officials say it is fine (CDC).
Don’t leave the house or shelter to get formula. Staying inside and breastfeeding is better (CDC).
Breastfeeding: if you were indoors with the doors and windows closed, keep breastfeeding (CDC).

If you were outside, two CDC pages say it differently. CDC’s Infant Feeding page: if you were outside in the affected area, consider stopping breastfeeding for a while and feed breast milk pumped and stored before the emergency, or formula; if you have neither, keep breastfeeding; to keep up your milk, express or pump regularly and throw that milk away; breastfeeding can start again when local health officials say, or after you leave the area and clean yourself off.

CDC’s Frequently Asked Questions page: if possible, nursing mothers who were near the affected area should stop breastfeeding for a while and switch to breast milk pumped and stored before the exposure, or formula, until they can be seen by a doctor; if no other food is available for the baby, keep breastfeeding.
Keep taking your medicine. Medicine that was indoors can be used; if the container was outdoors, wipe it off first (CDC).
Pet food in sealed containers can be used. Wipe the containers before opening them, and wash or wipe pet bowls, dishes and mats (CDC).
